2.text: After the ceremony, the mother proceeds to find a name for the child.

3.text: This is done by divination with a suspended object, which may be the

4.text: divinatory stone, or some part of the mother’s or child’s dress, such as a

5.text: boot or a cap. The mother, while holding the suspended object in her hands,
5.note: Printed as “Thé” with a stray raised mark over the e; the word is ordinary English “The” and the mark is print noise, not a diacritic — keyed without it.

6.text: enumerates, one by one, the names of all deceased relatives, saying with each

7.text: name, “This and this has come?” When the object loses its balance and
7.note: mz/ocr draft dropped the question mark before the closing quote; restored from the raster.

8.text: begins to swing, the name is selected. Then the people say aloud, “Such

9.text: and such a one has returned to us.”
9.note: Closing quote is curly per §1/§5.6; draft carried a straight ASCII quote.

10.text: This is more than a mere verbal formula. For instance, I met on the

11.text: Wolverene River a Reindeer Chukchee family who, two years before, had

12.text: lost their chief, who was much beloved by his sons and nephews. Immedi-

13.text: ately afterward the wife of the oldest son of the deceased man gave

14.text: birth to a son, to whom was given the name of his grandfather. He was

15.text: considered, in a way, as a re-incarnation of the deceased one, and therefore

16.text: was always spoken of as the house-master. At one time, when the youngest

17.text: and favorite daughter of the deceased one — but who, nevertheless, had a

18.text: violent temper — began to abuse her oldest sister, the mother said, “Tell the

19.text: house-master [meaning the small boy]. Let him try and make her silent.
19.note: Printed with square brackets, not parentheses, around the editorial gloss; draft misread the closing bracket plus period as “boyl.”

20.note: Draft appended a stray “?” after the period; the printed line ends with the closing curly quote only, no question mark.

21.text: In other cases the name is selected in quite different ways, frequently from

22.text: indications received in dreams. Thus, the mother accepts for the child the

23.text: name of the first object that comes to her sight after her delivery, or the

24.text: name of the first animal that crosses her path after leaving the tent. The

25.text: intention of this method is probably to mislead the “spirits,” who will not
25.note: Both quotes are curly in print; draft carried a straight opening apostrophe.

26.text: be able to recognize the child under the incidental name of the first thing

27.text: seen, selected by chance. Nevertheless, even in this case, the name selected

28.text: is often the name of a deceased relative, which, in days gone by, was chosen

29.text: in the same manner. Similar methods of naming children are used also by

31.text: Often the name fixed upon does not agree with the child, who then

32.text: grows slowly, and is sickly, or, as the Chukchee say, “It has heavy bones.”
32.note: Draft read “Ilt” for “It” and straight quotes for curly; both corrected from the raster.

33.text: Then a shaman, or a “knowing person,” is invited, who proceeds to change

34.text: the name. This process is sometimes repeated five or six times during the

35.text: first few years of the child’s life.

38.text: Incantation” (keimiˊtkin êˊwg̣an). It is performed by means of one or several

39.text: pieces of red hematite, which must be picked up on the seashore, close to

40.text: the water. The Chukchee call it “liver-stone.” In cases of necessity — for

41.text: instance, in winter-time, and especially among the Reindeer people of the

42.text: inland country — any other red stone may be used; but it must be taken

43.text: from the side of the hill lying in the direction of the sea.
